scales.name: Problematic Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence Scale – 9 items
scales.summary: A 9-item screener of problematic generative AI use modelled on the nine DSM-5 Internet Gaming Disorder criteria, validated in Chinese and US adults. Use it for cross-national prevalence studies or clinical-style screening of GenAI overuse.

subscales.name: (unidimensional)
subscales.description: One item per IGD criterion (past year): preoccupation, tolerance, withdrawal, persistence, escape, problems, deception, displacement, conflict.

psychometrics.structure: 31-item nine-dimension CFA (CFI .968, TLI .957, SRMR .027, RMSEA .080); 9-item short form CFA (CFI .948, TLI .931, RMSEA .045, SRMR .038); network analysis on the validation sample
psychometrics.reliability: α and ω computed (values not in the main text, likely in the supplement); CITC .67–.80
validity: Measurement invariance: configural and partial metric across nationality (4 parameters freed); full invariance up to latent means across gender

Criterion: positive correlations with rumination, stress, loneliness and ADHD symptoms, negative with self-esteem; linked to use frequency and emotionally supportive use; not correlated with GenAI literacy
Latent profile analysis: estimated 5–10% prevalence

samples.population: adults (Credamo and Prolific), exploratory phase (64 excluded)

scales.citation: Sun, H., Wu, D., Liu, W., Yao, M., & Yu, G. (2027). Emotionally vulnerable subtype of internet gaming disorder: Measuring and exploring the pathology of problematic generative AI use. Computers in Human Behavior, 186, 109116. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2026.109116
scales.authors: Haocan Sun; Di Wu; Weizi Liu; Mike Yao; Guoming Yu

scales.name: AI Addiction Scale – Screening Scale for Artificial Intelligence Addiction Diagnosis
scales.summary: A short Ukrainian screening tool for generative AI addiction risk. It has 10 scored items in two factors (socio-emotional and behavioral-cognitive dependence), a separate critical-thinking item, and cut-off scores. Use it for quick risk screening in student samples.
scales.target: Generative AI (items refer to 'AI'; 85.5% of the sample used ChatGPT)
scales.response: 5-point frequency scale (1 = never to 5 = always / very often)

subscales.name: Socio-Emotional Dependence
subscales.description: Preferring to confide in or talk to AI over people and turning to it under stress.

subscales.name: Behavioral-Cognitive Dependence
subscales.description: Accepting AI answers unchecked, anxiety or avoidance of tasks without AI, more time spent and hiding use.

subscales.name: Critical Thinking Indicator (+1)
subscales.description: A single reverse item (checking AI information against other sources) scored separately from the addiction index.

psychometrics.structure: Two factors for the 10 core items from EFA (KMO .790), revised from a hypothesized three-factor 11-item v3.0; no CFA
validity: Nomological: loneliness and stress predicted AI addiction (bootstrap mediation analyses)
Criterion: ROC against an external criterion (AUC = .733; Youden-optimal cut-off ≥18); Gaussian mixture modelling and K-means supported the cut-offs; 20.2% classified at risk

samples.population: university students who actively use generative AI

scales.citation: Chornomydz, A., Lukaniuk, M., & Oleshchuk, O. (2026). Development and psychometric validation of the screening scale for artificial intelligence addiction diagnosis (AIAS-10+1 v4.0). Psychological Journal, 12(3), 7–33. https://doi.org/10.31108/1.2026.12.3.1
scales.authors: Andrii Chornomydz; Mariana Lukaniuk; Oleksandra Oleshchuk

scales.name: AI Attachment Scale
scales.summary: Measures how attached people feel to the generative AI systems they use (e.g., ChatGPT, Replika): emotional closeness, using AI in place of people, and treating AI with regard. Useful for studies of AI companionship, loneliness and social substitution.
scales.target: Generative AI systems used most often (ChatGPT, Replika, DALL-E, DeepSeek and similar conversational systems)
scales.response: 5-point Likert (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

subscales.name: Emotional Closeness
subscales.description: Feeling that exchanges with AI are meaningful, familiar and comforting, and unease if AI became unavailable

subscales.name: Social Substitution
subscales.description: Turning to AI when there is no one to talk to or when feeling unsupported by people

subscales.name: Normative Regard
subscales.description: Treating AI respectfully, politely and considerately

psychometrics.structure: EFA in Singapore (n=339) and US (n=302) samples gave 15 items on 3 factors (58% and 70% variance). CFA in Study 4 (n=255): χ²(87)=187.77, CFI .96, TLI .95, RMSEA .06, SRMR .06, plus a higher-order model. Full scalar/residual invariance across sex; partial scalar and residual invariance across culture (Singapore vs US)
psychometrics.reliability: α .85–.94 for subscales, .95–.97 total; 1-week test–retest ICC .89 (r = .89; n = 234)
validity: Convergent: r = .77 with AI anthropomorphism and r = .72 with AI interaction positivity
Discriminant: near-zero correlations (|r| ≤ .08) with Big Five, pet attachment and parasocial attachment; Fornell–Larcker criterion satisfied
Measurement invariance across sex and culture (Singapore vs US)
Nomological: correlates with loneliness, social anxiety, anxious attachment, need fulfilment, positive affect and life satisfaction

samples.population: pilot item evaluation (30 Singapore students, 32 US Prolific adults)

scales.citation: Kasturiratna, K. T. A. S., & Hartanto, A. (2026). Attachment to artificial intelligence: Development of the AI Attachment Scale, construct validation, and the psychological mechanisms of human–AI attachment. Computers in Human Behavior Reports, 21, 100912. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chbr.2025.100912
scales.authors: K. T. A. Sandeeshwara Kasturiratna; Andree Hartanto

scales.name: AI Attachment Scale (Cheng & Yu)
scales.summary: Measures emotional bonds with AI chatbots such as ChatGPT: getting emotional support, distress when separated, and using the chatbot as a secure base. Useful in research on attachment to chatbots and on emotional design.

subscales.name: Emotional Support
subscales.description: Turning to the chatbot for comfort and emotional support

subscales.name: Separation Distress
subscales.description: Distress when the chatbot is unavailable

subscales.name: Secure Base
subscales.description: Using the chatbot as a secure base for exploring and acting

psychometrics.structure: EFA (N = 531) gave 15 items on 3 dimensions; CFA in a second sample (N = 375) supported the structure
validity: Nomological/predictive: anthropomorphism was the strongest predictor; general attachment anxiety predicted AI attachment positively (β = .44) and avoidance negatively (β = −.53); AI attachment predicted behavioural intentions (β = .50)

scales.citation: Cheng, N., & Yu, R. (2026). Measuring and understanding emotional attachment in human–AI relationships. Ergonomics, 1–20. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1080/00140139.2026.2622539
scales.authors: Nuo Cheng; Ruifeng Yu
scales.flag_reason: EFA and CFA in separate samples plus nomological relations are reported, but reliability could not be confirmed.

scales.name: AI Chatbot Emotional Dependence Scale
scales.summary: A brief 5-item scale of adolescents' emotional dependence on AI chatbots: turning to them for comfort, relief and feeling understood. Use it alongside instrumental dependence measures in youth mental-health research.
scales.response: 7-point Likert (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree)

subscales.name: (unidimensional)
subscales.description: Relying on an AI chatbot for comfort, emotional relief, perceived understanding and support when sad, stressed or lonely.

psychometrics.structure: One factor (6-item pool reduced to 5); EFA (n=2927; 69.07% variance, loadings .778–.864) and CFA (n=2928; CFI .98, TLI .95, SRMR .02)
validity: Convergent: AVE .65; loadings ≥ .73
Correlation r = .67 with Zhang et al.'s (2025) AI chatbot dependence scale
Measurement invariance: configural, metric and scalar across sex and educational stage

samples.population: adolescents from 7 middle and high schools in 5 provinces (Anhui, Hebei, Hubei, Guizhou, Shanxi); randomly split for EFA/CFA

scales.citation: Wei, X., Liu, D., & Cheung, H. N. (2026). Emotional dependence on AI chatbots: Development and validation of the AIED Scale [Preprint]. PsyArXiv. https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/yhetz_v1
scales.authors: Xiyu Wei; Dongyu Liu; Ho Nam Cheung

scales.name: AI Chatbots Acceptance and Perception Scale (AI Chatbots Usage Scale)
scales.summary: A multidimensional scale of higher-education students' acceptance of AI chatbots: ease of use, perceived usefulness, trust, and accessibility. Use it in education research on chatbot adoption; the Trust subscale covers confidence in the accuracy and integrity of chatbot responses.
scales.response: 5-point frequency scale (always to never)

subscales.name: Ease of Use
subscales.description: How easy AI chatbots are to use.

subscales.name: Perceived Usefulness
subscales.description: How useful chatbots are for learning.

subscales.name: Trust
subscales.description: Confidence in the accuracy, reliability, and integrity of AI chatbot responses.

subscales.name: Accessibility
subscales.description: Availability and access to AI chatbots.

psychometrics.structure: EFA (n=374) gave 4 factors, 42.48% variance; CFA (n=599) χ²/df=1.70, CFI=.979, TLI=.976, RMSEA=.034, GFI=.957
psychometrics.reliability: Total α/ω .927; Ease of Use .893, Usefulness .799, Trust .804, Accessibility .731 (ω .734)
validity: Convergent: AVE = .717, CR = .909
Discriminant: HTMT < .85 for all factor pairs; √AVE > inter-factor correlations (Fornell–Larcker)

scales.citation: Ibrahim, A. R., & Nemt-allah, M. A. (2026). Development and psychometric validation of the AI chatbots acceptance and perception scale for higher education students. Scientific Reports, 16, 22941. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-62798-4
scales.authors: Ashraf Ragab Ibrahim, Mohamed Ali Nemt-allah

scales.name: AI Dependence Scale for Chinese Undergraduates
scales.summary: A 22-item measure of university students' overreliance on (generative) AI for studying, covering emotional, functional and cognitive dependence and loss of control. Use it in higher-education research on academic AI overreliance.
scales.target: AI tools used for study, framed around generative AI such as ChatGPT (items say 'AI'; one refers to chat prompts)
scales.response: 5-point Likert (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree); mean-score bands: 1.00–2.49 low, 2.50–3.49 moderate, ≥3.50 high

subscales.name: Emotional dependence
subscales.description: Unease, anxiety or tension without AI help, and feeling calm or supported when using it.

subscales.name: Functional dependence
subscales.description: Delegating academic tasks to AI and feeling unable to manage them without it.

subscales.name: Cognitive dependence
subscales.description: Asking AI before thinking and letting it make judgments; perceived decline in independent thinking.

subscales.name: Loss of control
subscales.description: Failed attempts to cut down, difficulty stopping, and urges to use AI.

psychometrics.structure: Four factors; EFA (sample 1) and CFA (sample 2: χ²(203)=228.89, CFI .994, TLI .993, RMSEA .018, SRMR .052); competing models with fewer factors fit worse
validity: Content validity by expert I-CVI review and cognitive interviews
Convergent: AVE .53–.58
Discriminant: Fornell-Larcker criterion met (inter-factor r .21–.26)
Criterion: r = −.46 with academic self-efficacy
Behavioral indicators: r = .48 with variety of AI use, .37 with frequency, .33 with extent
Group differences by gender, year, major and use frequency

samples.population: undergraduates at one university in Southwest China (EFA)
undergraduates at one university in Southwest China (CFA)

scales.citation: Wu, H., Ni, H., Luo, W., & Wu, T. (2026). Development and validation of the AI dependence scale for Chinese undergraduates and a preliminary exploration. Frontiers in Psychology, 16, 1725393. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1725393
scales.authors: Houyu Wu; Haiyang Ni; Wenfu Luo; Tenglong Wu

scales.name: AI Information Literacy Scale
scales.summary: Measures how adults find, create and process, and critically assess information using generative AI tools, plus the ethics of doing so, grounded in information-behaviour theory. Use it in information-literacy, library or organisational research.
scales.target: Generative AI tools as information sources

subscales.name: Creation and processing
subscales.description: Creating and processing information with GenAI

subscales.name: Assessment and critique
subscales.description: Evaluating and critiquing GenAI-provided information

subscales.name: Seeking and retrieval
subscales.description: Seeking and retrieving information with GenAI

subscales.name: Ethics
subscales.description: Ethical information practices with GenAI

psychometrics.structure: Four components from principal components analysis (39 items); no CFA mentioned in the abstract
psychometrics.reliability: α .92–.96 for the three broad factors; α .73 for the 2-item ethics factor
validity: Expert review (43 → 40 items)
Group differences: higher scores among younger, more educated and more frequent AI users

scales.citation: Alon, L., & Levkovich, I. (2026). Information literacy in the age of generative tools: Development and validation of the AI Information Literacy Scale (AILIS). Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans, 7, Article 100254. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chbah.2026.100254
scales.authors: Lilach Alon; Inbar Levkovich
scales.venue: Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans
scales.flag_reason: Structure comes from principal components analysis only (no CFA), and validity rests on group differences.

scales.name: AI Learning Strategies Scale
scales.summary: A 12-item scale of how often learners use AI tools, mainly generative AI like ChatGPT, strategically to plan, carry out and reflect on their learning (self-regulated learning with AI). Use it to study individual differences in strategic AI use for studying.
scales.target: AI tools used for learning (generative AI such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, plus other AI learning apps)
scales.response: 5-point frequency scale (1 = never to 5 = always)

subscales.name: Forethought
subscales.description: Using AI to set goals and plan learning before starting

subscales.name: Performance
subscales.description: Using AI to organise, process and monitor learning during the task

subscales.name: Self-Reflection
subscales.description: Using AI to evaluate and reflect on one's learning afterwards

psychometrics.structure: Study 2 EFA (n=320): 3 factors; Studies 3–4 CFA (n=285, n=270) confirmed the 3-factor model
psychometrics.reliability: α .94–.95 total (subscales .88–.92); 1-week test-retest ICC(2,1) .80 total, .66–.76 subscales
validity: Measurement invariance across sex (multi-group CFA)
Convergent and discriminant validity (AVE/Fornell–Larcker)
Nomological network: self-efficacy, autonomous motivation, mastery goals, Big Five, AI attitudes, AI use, AI fatigue
Criterion validity: predicts richer self-regulated-learning content in a writing task

scales.citation: Lau, G. R., Liow, C. J. M., Gasevic, D., & Hartanto, A. (2026). AI Learning Strategies Scale: Development and validation for individual differences in self-regulated learning with AI [Preprint]. PsyArXiv. https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/jqxh9_v1
scales.authors: Gabriel Rongyang Lau; Caresse Jia Min Liow; Dragan Gasevic; Andree Hartanto

scales.name: AI-giarism Scale – Turkish version
scales.summary: A scenario-based scale that asks university students how far various uses of generative AI in assignments count as academic misconduct. The uses range from copying AI output to AI-augmented writing to little or no AI reliance. Use it to study students' views on the ethics of AI-assisted plagiarism in Turkish-speaking samples.
scales.target: generative AI use in academic assignments (AI-assisted plagiarism)
scales.response: 5-point agreement (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree) that each described action constitutes academic misconduct

subscales.name: Plagiaristic AI use
subscales.description: Scenarios where AI output is copied or used without proper attribution

subscales.name: AI-augmented writing
subscales.description: Scenarios where GenAI output is verified, edited and combined with the student's own work, with AI use disclosed

subscales.name: No AI reliance
subscales.description: Scenarios with only minimal AI use (grammar check, source search) or none

psychometrics.structure: EFA (PAF, oblimin): 3 factors, 59.7% of variance. CFA (N=426): χ²(41)=193.98, CFI .937, TLI .916, SRMR .052, RMSEA .094. The paper's EFA table and its factor labels do not line up cleanly; subscale item counts follow the CFA table.
validity: Convergent validity: AVE .56–.64
Factor intercorrelations reported (.04–.55)
No gender differences (Mann–Whitney U)

scales.citation: Gökçearslan, Ş., Mumcu, F., Chiu, T., & Lavicza, Z. (2026). Measuring AI-giarism: A validation study and dimensional exploration of the scale in Turkish. Journal of Learning and Teaching in Digital Age, 11(1), 111–118. https://doi.org/10.53850/joltida.1762390
scales.authors: Şahin Gökçearslan; Filiz Mumcu; Thomas Chiu; Zsolt Lavicza
scales.venue: Journal of Learning and Teaching in Digital Age

scales.name: ATRAI-LLM questionnaire (Attitudes Toward LLMs in Clinical Setting)
scales.summary: Measures physicians' attitudes toward LLM-based chatbots used as a clinical reference tool, covering willingness to use, implementation outlook, and hopes and fears. Use it to survey clinicians before or during LLM roll-outs.
scales.target: LLM-based chatbots answering clinical queries (e.g., YandexGPT, GigaChat in the Moscow health system)
scales.response: Mixed: 5-point Likert (1 = extremely negative to 5 = extremely positive), multiple-choice/multiple-response and 5-point items. 8 background items and 11 main items, of which 9 are scored (total 0–36).

subscales.name: Willingness to Use
subscales.description: Views that encourage or discourage using an LLM assistant: wide implementation, trust in EHR-retrieved information, who should pay, workload change (score 0–16)

subscales.name: Implementation Perspective
subscales.description: Most trustworthy topics, most-used functions and expected changes in practice (score 0–12)

subscales.name: Hopes and Fears
subscales.description: Expected LLM-related changes in professional status and salary (score 0–8)

psychometrics.structure: Domains identified by hierarchical clustering of item correlations. CFA supported three factors (RMSEA .05, CFI .97, TLI .96, SRMR .03); one-factor model fit poorly.
psychometrics.reliability: α .770 (95% CI .731–.800); ωt .830; no test–retest (the authors argue it is inappropriate for rapidly changing LLMs)
validity: Criterion: Spearman ρ = .68 between total score and a visual analogue scale of attitude toward LLMs
Face and content validity via focus group and expert review

samples.population: Physicians from medical organizations of the Moscow Department of Health (71.7% had prior LLM-chatbot use)

scales.citation: Reshetnikov, R. V., Vasilev, Y. A., Shumskaya, Y. F., Akhmedzyanova, D. A., Alymova, Y. A., Vladzymyrskyy, A. V., Tyrov, I. A., Omelyanskaya, O. V., & Blokhin, I. A. (2026). Development and validation of the ATRAI questionnaire to assess attitudes toward large language models in clinical setting (ATRAI-LLM). European Journal of Investigation in Health, Psychology and Education, 16(7), 94. https://doi.org/10.3390/ejihpe16070094
scales.authors: Roman V. Reshetnikov; Yuriy A. Vasilev; Yuliya F. Shumskaya; Dina A. Akhmedzyanova; Yulya A. Alymova; Anton V. Vladzymyrskyy; Ilya A. Tyrov; Olga V. Omelyanskaya; Ivan A. Blokhin
scales.venue: European Journal of Investigation in Health, Psychology and Education

scales.name: Academic Integrity and Generative AI Short Questionnaire
scales.summary: A 15-item questionnaire on how university students approach academic integrity when using generative AI. It covers normative, ethical use (including awareness of misuse risks) and legitimate use of GenAI to support academic writing. Use it for quick surveys of GenAI-related integrity attitudes in higher education.
scales.target: Generative AI in higher-education writing and assessment

subscales.name: Normative integrity in AI use
subscales.description: Ethical use of GenAI and awareness of the risks of misuse (merges two original dimensions)

subscales.name: Support for academic writing
subscales.description: Using GenAI legitimately to support academic writing

psychometrics.structure: EFA and CFA with robust DWLS for ordinal items. The original 17 items in 3 dimensions (ethical use of AI, awareness of misuse risks, support for academic writing) were refined to 15 items in 2 correlated factors with adequate fit.
psychometrics.reliability: 'High internal consistency' per abstract; coefficients not seen
validity: Convergent validity supported
Discriminant validity acceptable but borderline
Preliminary measurement invariance across gender (configural model absolute fit not optimal)

samples.country: Peru (inferred from author affiliations; not stated in abstract)

scales.citation: Garro-Aburto, L. L., Chávez-Díaz, J. M., Hinojosa Salazar, C. A., Llerena Espinoza, E. M., & Sánchez Sandoval, S. P. (2026). Academic integrity and generative artificial intelligence in higher education: Psychometric validation of a short questionnaire. Education Sciences, 16(7), 1125. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci16071125
scales.authors: Luzmila Lourdes Garro-Aburto; Jorge Miguel Chávez-Díaz; Carlos Alberto Hinojosa Salazar; Edith María Llerena Espinoza; Sara Pamela Sánchez Sandoval

scales.name: Acceptability Scale for the Use of LLMs by Project Teams
scales.summary: A 13-item scale of project professionals' before-use (a priori) acceptability of LLMs, measured through beliefs about what LLMs and prompt engineering can do for project work. Use it for organisational or project-management diagnostics of LLM adoption.
scales.target: Large language models (and prompt engineering) in project management
scales.response: 5-point Likert (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

subscales.name: Intention/Predisposition
subscales.description: Beliefs that AI/LLM tools improve decisions, forecasting, resource allocation and stakeholder management in projects

subscales.name: Trust/Perceived Benefit
subscales.description: Beliefs about how prompt quality and engineering shape LLM output quality and domain adaptation

psychometrics.structure: Polychoric EFA and CFA on the same sample; 17 items reduced to 13 on two correlated factors (r = .50). CFA (17-item model): CFI .979, TLI .976, RMSEA .060
validity: Content validation (2 AI experts, cognitive pretest with 3 project managers)
Convergent validity: AVE .543 / .518 (13-item recalculation)
Discriminant validity: Fornell–Larcker met; HTMT .587
Nomological: Spearman ρ = .197 (p = .015) Trust/Perceived Benefit and .153 (p = .058) Intention/Predisposition with LLM usage frequency

scales.citation: Carvalho, M. Z. de, Penha, R., Vils, L., Bizarrias, F. S., & Serra, F. A. R. (2026). Acceptability scale for the use of large language models (LLMs) by project teams: Development and preliminary validation. Systems, 14(4), 366. https://doi.org/10.3390/systems14040366
scales.authors: Carvalho, M. Z. de, Penha, R., Vils, L., Bizarrias, F. S., & Serra, F. A. R.

scales.name: Agentic Engagement with AI Scale
scales.summary: A 16-item scale of how actively students steer their learning with generative AI: directing the AI, critically integrating its output, checking other sources and adjusting through reflection. Use it to study student agency in AI-assisted learning.

subscales.name: Adaptive Direction
subscales.description: Steering AI interactions toward one's learning goals

subscales.name: Critical Integration
subscales.description: Critically evaluating and integrating AI output

subscales.name: Cross-Source Inquiry
subscales.description: Checking AI output against other sources

subscales.name: Reflective Calibration
subscales.description: Adjusting one's AI use through reflection

psychometrics.structure: 28 items from interviews (n=26); expert review; EFA (n=340); CFA (n=256); final 4 factors, 16 items
validity: Criterion validity checking
Expert review (content)

scales.citation: Dai, Y., Liu, S., Zhou, S., Lai, S., Liu, A., & Lim, C. P. (2026). Redefining and measuring student agency in AI-assisted learning: Development and validation of the agentic engagement with AI (AE-AI) scale. Computers & Education, 253, 105687. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2026.105687
scales.authors: Yun Dai; Suya Liu; Sihan Zhou; Sichen Lai; Ang Liu; Cher Ping Lim

scales.name: Apprehension Towards Large Language Models Scale (one of the Four AI Apprehension Scales)
scales.summary: An 8-item scale of how much more reassurance people would need before feeling comfortable with LLM products. It covers the perceived morality of LLM makers, the social awkwardness of using LLMs in public, and their predictability. Parallel versions exist for general, personal and institutional AI, so you can compare apprehension across AI types.
scales.response: 11-point scale (0 = 'Nothing more needed' to 10 = 'A great deal more needed'); common stem 'I think further conditions are necessary for me…'

subscales.name: Implied Malice
subscales.description: Needing more before feeling that LLM makers take morality seriously and that the products are designed and run ethically

subscales.name: Undesirability
subscales.description: Needing more before feeling normal and at ease interacting with LLM products in public

subscales.name: Unpredictability
subscales.description: Needing more before feeling that LLM products work as described and have clear purposes and goals

psychometrics.structure: CFA of the 3-factor model for the LLM version: CFI .99, TLI .98, SRMR .04, RMSEA .085 (90% CI .067–.103). The 3-factor model fit better than 1- and 2-factor alternatives. Standardized LLM loadings .78–.97. Network analysis also reported.
psychometrics.reliability: Reported across the four parallel scales: Implied Malice Spearman-Brown/α .86–.94; Undesirability and Unpredictability α .89–.97; CR .90–.97; AVE > .73; H .56–.81
validity: Convergent: ATAI Acceptance (negative) and ATAI Fear (positive) predict LLM apprehension (robust regression; R² .201, rising to .219 with openness)
Discriminant: Fornell-Larcker criterion met; inter-factor r < .82; 3-factor model beats 1- and 2-factor models
LLM apprehension shares 67.9% of variance with general-AI apprehension, showing partial distinctiveness

scales.citation: Yankouskaya, A., Almourad, M. B., Liebherr, M., Rahman, M. M., AlShakhsi, S., & Ali, R. (2026). The four artificial intelligence apprehension scales: Apprehension towards personal AI, general AI, institutional AI, and large language models [Preprint]. Research Square. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-9018418/v1
scales.authors: Ala Yankouskaya; Mohamed Basel Almourad; Magnus Liebherr; Mohammad Mominur Rahman; Sameha AlShakhsi; Raian Ali

scales.name: Artificial Intelligence Use Motivations Scale
scales.summary: A 22-item measure of why people use generative AI such as ChatGPT. It covers 11 motives, including usefulness, fun, companionship, escaping social anxiety, seeing AI as human-like, and prestige. Use it to study which motives drive healthy versus problematic GenAI use.
scales.response: 5-point Likert (strongly disagree to strongly agree)

subscales.name: Perceived usefulness
subscales.description: Using AI because it improves task performance

subscales.name: Self-efficacy
subscales.description: Confidence in completing tasks with AI

subscales.name: Availability
subscales.description: AI is easy for anyone to use without special skills

subscales.name: Perceived trust
subscales.description: Believing AI output is correct and reliable

subscales.name: Perceived safety
subscales.description: Not worrying about data exposure when using AI

subscales.name: Seeking pleasure and fun
subscales.description: Using AI because it is enjoyable

subscales.name: Social interaction
subscales.description: AI as companionship, like talking to a friend

subscales.name: Escaping social anxiety and judgment
subscales.description: Preferring AI to avoid anxiety or judgment from people

subscales.name: Anthropomorphism and empathy
subscales.description: Seeing AI as human-like, with intentions or awareness

subscales.name: Tech-based social prestige
subscales.description: Using AI to look knowledgeable and up to date

subscales.name: Personal innovativeness
subscales.description: Valuing AI's creative, novel suggestions

psychometrics.structure: EFA (n = 648) gave 6 factors. A theory-based 11-factor CFA fit well: χ²/df 1.53, RMSEA .028, CFI .986, TLI .979.
validity: Full measurement invariance across gender (multi-group CFA)

Convergent/discriminant: compensatory-affective motives were related to problematic ChatGPT use, social anxiety and digital addiction; competence-adaptive motives were related to self-esteem and social support
Incremental: motives explained an additional 15% of variance in problematic ChatGPT use

scales.citation: Akbari, M., Mollaali Farkhani, S., Golmohammadi, M., Mirjalili, M., Yasaghi, F., Hatampour, R., & Griffiths, M. D. (2026). scales.name: Critical Thinking in AI Use Scale
scales.summary: A 13-item measure of how much people check what generative AI tells them, want to understand how AI models work and fail, and think about what relying on AI means. Use it to study fact-checking of AI output, over-reliance, and responsible GenAI use.
scales.response: 5-point Likert (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

subscales.name: Verification
subscales.description: Checking the sources and content of AI outputs rather than accepting them at face value.

subscales.name: Motivation
subscales.description: Wanting to understand how AI models work and where they fail.

subscales.name: Reflection
subscales.description: Reflecting on the ethical, societal and personal implications of relying on AI.

psychometrics.structure: Study 1: content validation (24 naive judges). Study 2: EFA (n=270) reduced 27 items to 13 across 3 factors (RMSEA=.04, TLI=.98, CFI=.99). Study 3: correlated and higher-order CFA (n=376), χ²(62)=131.75, CFI=1.00, TLI=1.00, RMSEA=.06, SRMR=.05. Study 4 (n=290): CFA χ²(62)=144.22, CFI=.97, TLI=.96, RMSEA=.07

validity: Sex invariance: configural, metric, scalar and residual (all ΔCFI ≤ .01)
Convergent validity (AVE .59–.77), discriminant evidence, and a nomological network: openness, extraversion, positive affect, AI use frequency; weak link with CRT

Criterion (Study 6): higher scores predicted more frequent and varied verification strategies, better veracity-judgement accuracy in a GPT-powered chatbot fact-checking task, and deeper reflection on responsible AI

subscales.name: AI Use and Awareness

subscales.name: Technological Knowledge (TK)

scales.target: Generative AI (in assessment and feedback contexts)
scales.response: 5-point Likert (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

scales.response: 5-point Likert (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

subscales.name: GenAI ethics (AIE)
subscales.description: Protecting sensitive data and teaching safe, responsible GenAI use (Domain 1)

subscales.name: GenAI for student interaction (GSI)
subscales.description: Using GenAI to make classes interactive and engaging (Domain 2: teaching)

subscales.name: GenAI for learning design (GLD)
subscales.description: Creating courseware and learning resources with GenAI (Domain 2)

subscales.name: GenAI for assessment (GAS)
subscales.description: Designing and running assessment in GenAI-supported settings (Domain 2)

subscales.name: GenAI for research design (GRD)
subscales.description: Using GenAI to formulate topics, plan research and choose methods (Domain 3: research)

subscales.name: GenAI data analysis (GDA)

subscales.name: GenAI and professional development (GPD)

validity: Content validity by educational technology experts; pilot with 25 students

Criterion validity supported

scales.name: Generative AI Reliance Types Scale
scales.summary: A 20-item scale of how students rely on generative AI when writing: strategic (planned use and checking of outputs), instrumental, dependent, and dialogic reliance. Use it to tell productive reliance on GenAI apart from over-reliance in writing courses.
scales.target: Generative AI tools used for academic writing (e.g., ChatGPT)
scales.response: 7-point Likert (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree); authors recommend a 5-point format for the next version

subscales.name: Strategic – Deliberate Use
subscales.description: Planned, purposeful use of GenAI guided by writing goals.

subscales.name: Strategic – Critical Evaluation
subscales.description: Checking facts, logic and bias in GenAI text and revising it extensively.

subscales.name: Instrumental
subscales.description: Using GenAI as an efficiency tool for specific subtasks (outlines, rephrasing, summaries, prompts).

subscales.name: Dependent
subscales.description: Accepting GenAI output by default with little revision or questioning, and feeling uneasy without it.

subscales.name: Dialogic
subscales.description: Iterative, conversational co-writing and brainstorming with GenAI.

validity: Scalar measurement invariance across gender, first-generation status and STEM/non-STEM major
Strategic reliance correlated with AI literacy (composite r = .61; core r = .51; prior exposure r = .55)
Reliance types differed across writing processes and outcomes; response-process evidence from 14 interviews

subscales.name: Learning

subscales.name: Development

Independent-samples t-tests, item-total/item-remainder correlations and inter-factor correlations

scales.summary: An 18-item scale of how much mental effort second-language writers spend when writing with generative AI chatbots. scales.target: generative AI chatbots (e.g., ChatGPT, Bing Chat, DeepSeek) in L2 writing
scales.response: 7-point mental-effort rating (1 = very, very low to 7 = very, very high mental effort)

subscales.name: Prompt Management
subscales.description: Effort spent phrasing, refining and managing prompts

subscales.name: Critical Evaluation
subscales.description: Effort judging the accuracy and quality of AI output

subscales.name: Integrative Synthesis

subscales.name: Authorial Core Processing
subscales.description: Effort on one's own ideas, voice and authorship

non-English-major students at a different university (CFA)

scales.name: Conversational AI Dependence Scale
scales.summary: A 20-item, addiction-framework measure of conversational AI dependence in Chinese college students, covering uncontrollability, withdrawal, mood modification and negative impacts. Use it when you want a detailed, symptom-style profile of chatbot dependence in students.
scales.target: Conversational AI (chatbots, intelligent assistants, LLM-based CAI)
scales.response: 6-point Likert (1 = completely disagree to 6 = completely agree); 'In the past year' reference

subscales.name: Uncontrollability
subscales.description: Salience, tolerance and using CAI longer or more often than intended.

subscales.name: Withdrawal symptoms
subscales.description: Irritability, anxiety, loss or helplessness when CAI is unavailable.

subscales.name: Mood modification
subscales.description: Using CAI to relieve negative emotions, irritability or loneliness.

subscales.name: Negative impact
subscales.description: Harms to studies, social relationships, hobbies and independent thinking.

psychometrics.structure: Four factors; EFA (N=547, 74.41% variance) then CFA (N=687; χ²/df 4.39, CFI .92, TLI .91, RMSEA .07, SRMR .06)

Discriminant: Fornell–Larcker criterion met (inter-factor r .50–.77 < √AVE)

Predictive/nomological (Study 3): predicted sleep problems, functional difficulties, depression, anxiety and stress, and lower subjective wellbeing

Discriminant validity

validity: Convergent validity: AVE .67–.75, loadings .74–.90
Discriminant validity argued from inter-factor r .81–.83 (< .90)
Content validity via expert review

subscales.name: User Control and Autonomy

scales.name: Experiences in Human-AI Relationships Scale
scales.summary: Applies adult attachment theory to relationships with generative AI such as ChatGPT. It measures attachment anxiety (needing reassurance and affection from AI) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with emotional closeness to AI).
scales.target: Generative AI (ChatGPT chosen as the reference system); items refer to 'AI'
scales.response: 7-point Likert (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree)

subscales.name: Attachment anxiety toward AI
subscales.description: Needing shows of affection, intimacy and reassurance from AI

subscales.name: Attachment avoidance toward AI
subscales.description: Preferring not to open up to, or be too close to, AI

psychometrics.structure: 20-item pool; EFA (principal axis, varimax) in pilot study 2 (N = 63) gave 2 factors and 7 items (61.66% variance); CFA in the main study (N = 242): χ²(13) = 15.47, CFI .992, RMSEA .028

scales.response: 5-point agreement scale (agree, somewhat agree, neutral, somewhat disagree, disagree; scored 5–1); construct scores are sums of 3 items

subscales.name: Fear
subscales.description: Fear about GenAI, e.g., being displaced in one's future healthcare job

subscales.name: Anxiety
subscales.description: Anxiety about GenAI's role in one's career and training

subscales.name: Mistrust

subscales.name: Ethics

scales.summary: An 11-item measure of dependency on generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Replika, DALL-E) with three facets: cognitive preoccupation, negative consequences and withdrawal. Good for adult or student samples when you want a short, well-validated multidimensional dependency score.

scales.name: Semantic Differential Scale for Affective and Cognitive AI Trust
scales.summary: A 27-item set of adjective-pair (semantic differential) scales measuring cognitive trust (18 items) and affective trust (9 items) in AI agents. It was built with LLM-powered conversational agents in mind. Use it when you need to separate emotional trust in a chatbot from competence-based trust.
scales.target: AI agents / LLM-powered conversational agents (validation used ChatGPT-generated chatbot conversations)
scales.response: Semantic differential (bipolar adjective pairs); 5-step (−2 to +2) in development, 7-point (−3 to +3) in validation studies

subscales.name: Cognitive trust
subscales.description: Perceived reliability, competence, rationality, transparency and integrity of the AI agent (e.g., unreliable–reliable, incompetent–competent).

subscales.name: Affective trust
subscales.description: Emotional warmth and care shown by the agent (e.g., apathetic–empathetic, rude–cordial, impatient–patient).

psychometrics.structure: Development: EFA on 33 adjective pairs (n=151, 302 responses) gave 2 factors (43% and 23% variance) after removing 6 cross-loading pairs. Study A: CFA (DWLS) excellent fit (CFI 1.000, TLI 1.003, RMSEA .000, SRMR .038). Study B: EFA with the MDMT moral trust items retained 3 factors (70% variance).
validity: Concurrent validity with a single-item general trust measure: development r = .881 (cognitive), .253 (affective); Study A r = .546 and .486
Construct validity: scales were sensitive to manipulated cognitive and affective trustworthiness in ChatGPT-generated conversations
Discriminant validity from MDMT moral trust (Study B): separate factor, and moral trust did not predict general trust
